readerTitle: The workshop is profitable. How much of that profit comes with it?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (팔레트·목재 상자 제조 공방 인수 + 물류 배차용 구독 소프트웨어 매물) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 기존 사업을 산다는 것은 과거의 이익이 아니라, 주인이 떠난 뒤에도 남는 이익을 사는 것이다.
misconception: 흑자인 사업을 사면 장부에 적힌 이익이 그대로 새 주인의 것이 된다.

sources.text: 소규모 사업 인수 실사의 일반 개념 (주인 노동 포함 이익, 고객 집중도, 인수 후 인계 기간, 성과 연동 잔금)
모든 인물, 매물, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: '이익의 3배'라는 가격 배수는 설명용 가정이며 실제 시장 평균 배수를 뜻하지 않습니다. 업종·규모·시기에 따라 크게 다르므로 카드에 시장 수치처럼 쓰지 않았습니다.
성과 연동 잔금(earnout), 인계 계약 등은 개념만 설명했고 국가별 법률·세무 조언은 하지 않았습니다. Watch out 카드에 전문가 검토를 권하는 문장만 넣었습니다.

cards.title: The workshop is profitable. How much of that profit comes with it?
body: You have savings and want to own a business. A broker sends a listing: a pallet and wooden crate workshop, 28 years old, eight staff, steady orders. The owner, Frank, is retiring.
Profit last year: **$180,000**. Asking price: $540,000, or three years of profit. It looks like a safe buy. Four decisions will tell you how safe.

image.label: A small workshop stacked with wooden pallets, a for-sale sign at the door
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 나무 팔레트와 상자가 쌓인 작은 공방 외관, 문 앞에 'For sale' 팻말. 안쪽에 지게차 한 대와 작업자 실루엣. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you check first?
body: You get two weeks to look at the books and the shop floor before making an offer.

options.text: How much of the $180,000 depends on Frank's own unpaid work
options.feedback: You learn Frank works 55 hours a week and pays himself no salary. Replacing him with a manager costs about $70,000, so the profit a non-working owner keeps is closer to $110,000.

options.text: The age and condition of the saws and the forklift
options.feedback: Useful, and old equipment can mean surprise bills. But machines are easy to see and price. The bigger gap in this deal is hidden in the profit figure.

options.text: Prices of similar workshops for sale nearby
options.feedback: Comparing prices feels careful, but it tells you nothing about whether this $180,000 is real for you. You could pay a fair multiple of the wrong number.

cards.title: Say you chose A. Then you read the customer list.
body: One regional furniture maker buys **45%** of everything the workshop makes. It has ordered every month for 12 years. The next biggest customer buys 8%.

options.text: Walk away. One customer is too much risk
options.feedback: Safe, but you may drop a good business over a problem you could have priced in. Heavy reliance on one customer is a reason to dig, not always to leave.

options.text: Ask to meet that customer before you make an offer
options.feedback: The furniture maker's buyer is friendly and honest: "We order here because of Frank. We'd give a new owner a fair try." Now you know the loyalty is to a person, not the workshop.

options.text: Relax. Twelve years of orders proves they'll stay
options.feedback: Past loyalty was earned by the old owner. If it leaves with him, nearly half your sales go too, and you won't find out until after you've paid.

cards.title: Say you chose B. Frank wants to leave on closing day.
body: He knows every customer, every supplier and which wood warps in damp weather. None of it is written down. He plans to move to the coast the week the sale closes.

options.text: Pay the full price and learn on the job
options.feedback: You pay for $180,000 of profit and inherit the relationships of someone who just left. If the big customer drifts away, the price is already spent.

options.text: Ask Frank to stay six months, paid, and tie part of the price to the big customer staying
options.feedback: Frank introduces you to buyers and teaches the crew to run without him. Paying part of the price later, only if sales hold, shares the risk with the seller.

options.text: Offer 20% less and let him go
options.feedback: A lower price helps, but it doesn't move the know-how into your hands. You'd save money and still face the hardest year alone.

cards.title: Say you chose B. The broker sends a second listing.
body: A small online tool that truck dispatchers pay for monthly to plan routes. About 400 subscribers, one founder, profit also around $110,000. The founder wants to sell and start something new.
Before comparing it with the workshop, what do you check first?

options.text: How fast sign-ups grew in the last three months
options.feedback: Growth is nice, but a steady small business lives on the customers it keeps. A burst of sign-ups can hide many quiet cancellations.

options.text: How many subscribers cancel each month, and who else can maintain the code
options.feedback: This is Frank's workshop again in digital form. Cancellations show whether customers stay without the founder's attention, and the code is his "know-how in his head."

options.text: Nothing much. Software costs little to run, so the profit is safe
options.feedback: Low running costs don't make profit transferable. If the founder was the only person who could fix the product, his unpaid work is part of the profit.

cards.softwareNote: In software, the owner's hidden labor is often support, bug fixes and keeping key accounts happy. Ask the founder for a normal week's calendar, not just the revenue chart.

cards.title: You buy the profit that survives the seller leaving.
body: Call it **transferable profit**: what the business earns once the old owner, and everything tied to him, is gone. At the same multiple of three, the workshop is worth about $330,000, not $540,000.

breakdown.label: A manager to do Frank's job
breakdown.detail: The owner's work is a real cost

breakdown.label: Transferable profit
breakdown.detail: Before any risk from the 45% customer

cards.callout: Three common leaks: the owner's own labor, customers loyal to a person, and know-how nobody wrote down.
cards.softwareNote: The same check applies to the route-planning tool: subtract what it would cost to pay someone to do the founder's job.

cards.title: Checking reduces risk. It doesn't remove it.
body: A careful review can still miss things. A key employee may quit. A big customer may change suppliers for reasons unrelated to you.
Paying part of the price later sounds tidy but can cause arguments over how sales are counted. Write the terms clearly and have a lawyer and an accountant review the deal where you live.
And a flaw is not always a reason to walk away. A business with problems can be a good buy at the right price.

cards.title: Buy what stays, not what was.
body: Each decision in the story ties to an idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1 → The owner's time trap:** the seller's unpaid hours are a cost you inherit
**Decision 2 → Buying vs starting:** buying gets you customers only if they transfer
**Decision 3 → Buying vs starting:** a paid handover moves the relationships and the know-how
**Decision 4 → Small business vs startup:** judge a steady business by who stays, not how fast it grows
cards.callout: **Try it today:** for your own business, list what would leave if you stepped away for three months. That list is what a buyer would discount.
